newsitem.title: USA: Nike profits jump 24 percent; splits stock.
newsitem.headline: Nike profits jump 24 percent; splits stock.

text.p: Nike Inc., the world's largest maker of athletic footwear, Monday reported a 24 percent jump in first quarter profits, reflecting strong demand for its shoes and apparel around the world.
The Beaverton, Ore.-based company also announced a two-for-one stock split, its second in two years.
News of the company's better-than-expected results, coupled with the stock split, sent shares of Nike soaring on Wall Street as investors sought to cash in on the company's positive outlook.

"One year ago, we approved a two-for-one stock split. At that time, I cited the growing power of the Nike brand as strong evidence of our outstanding financial performance," said company Chairman Philip Knight.

"That brand strength, which many thought was nearing its peak last year, continues to grow unabated in fiscal 1997, propelling Nike to the best quarter in our history, record futures orders, and another stock split for our shareholders."

For the three months ended Aug. 31, Nike earned $226.1 million, or $1.53 a share, up from $182.1 million or $1.25 a share a year ago. Revenues jumped 34 percent to $2.28 billion from $1.70 billion last year.
The profit exceeded the First Call consensus estimate of $1.51 a share, prompting many Wall Street analysts to boost their estimates for the year.
Nike attributed the strong first quarter results to robust demand for its athletic footware and apparel, both in the United States and abroad.

U.S. athletic footwear and apparel revenues totaled $1.35 billion in the first quarter, up 39 percent from a year ago. Sales of men's basketball shoes, the company's biggest category, rose 48 percent to more than $200 million in the quarter. Men's running shoe sales were up 67 percent while women's sports shoes jumped 58 percent.
Overseas, Nike reported equally strong results, with international athletic footwear and apparel revenues rising 35 percent last quarter to $780.9 million.

The company said worldwide orders for athletic footwear and apparel scheduled for delivery between September and January, known as futures orders, were at a record $3.5 billion, 66 percent higher than for the same period last year.

"The strength of the Nike brand is clearly evident in the U.S. market where both our footwear and apparel are experiencing outstanding sell-through at retail," Knight said. "In footwear, our men's basketball business in the U.S. grew 48 percent in the first quarter, an exceptional number given our dominant position in that market."
"Nike's brand presence outside the U.S. market continues to develop dramatically," he said.

Nike President Tom Clarke said as impressive as the company's results were last quarter, sales would have been even higher if not for a warehouse fire in June that shut the company's Memphis, Tenn. distribution facility.
In a conference call with analysts and reporters, Clarke said the shutdown cost Nike $40 million in lost sales for the quarter as the company struggled to keep up with demand.
He said most of the shortfall would be made up by the end of the current quarter.

Nike said the two-for-one stock split in both Nike Class A and Class B common shares would be in the form of a 100 percent stock dividend to be paid Oct. 23 to shareholders of record at the close of business Oct. 11.
Following the news, Nike's class B shares leaped $2.875 to $122.125 on the New York Stock Exchange with several analysts raising their earnings' estimates for the coming year.

Goldman Sachs analyst Margaret Mager raised her estimate for fiscal 1997 to $5.30 a share from $5, compared with $3.77 in fiscal 1996. For fiscal 1998 the brokerage raised its estimate to $6.30 a share, Mager said.

Nike's subsidiaries include Bauer Inc., the world's largest maker of hockey equipment; Cole Haan, a manufacturer of men's and women's dress and casual shoes and Sports Specialties Corp., a headwear manufacturer.
